document.title: Post-Conference Comments of National Grid plc o/b/o National Grid Ventures re PJM Governance and Stakeholder Reforms
document.group: PJM governance and stakeholder reform vote

pages.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
 
PJM Governance and Stakeholder Reforms  
) 
 
Docket No. AD26-7-000 
 
 
POST-CONFERENCE COMMENTS OF NATIONAL GRID 
 
National Grid plc, on behalf of its competitive energy development corporation, National 
Grid Ventures (“NGV”), respectfully submits these comments in response to the Notice 
Requesting Post-Conference Comments (“Notice”), issued by the Federal Energy Regulatory 
Commission (“FERC” or “Commission”) on July 30, 2026, in the above-referenced docket, 
following the Commission’s July 23, 2026 Commissioner-led technical conference to discuss 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s (“PJM”) governance and stakeholder processes.  NGV is a voting 
member of PJM in the “Other Supplier” sector and is an active participant in PJM’s competitive 
transmission processes.  NGV appreciates the Commission’s focus on identifying and evaluating 
concrete, actionable reforms to improve PJM’s ability to address operational and market needs in 
a timely and efficient manner.  To that end, below please find NGV’s responses to the questions 
presented in the Appendix to the Notice regarding PJM’s Board of Directors independence, 
Federal Power Act section 205 filing rights, stakeholder process, and state participation.   
PJM Board Independence 
 
Questions/Comments 
Yes No 
1) 
Should Board members’ terms be extended to five or more years? 
X 
 
 
Comments: NGV supports an extension of Board member terms to 4 to 6 years.  Longer 
terms will support continuity during a period of extraordinary industry transformation, 
strengthen institutional memory, and reinforce Board independence.  The terms of the 
Board members should remain staggered.

2 
 
 
Questions/Comments 
Yes No 
2) 
Should there be a maximum number of years that a Board member may 
serve (e.g., 10 years)? 
X 
 
 
Comments: If terms are extended to 4 to 6 years, NGV supports capping a Board 
member to the number of terms that equate to 12 years of service.  This brings the 
current 15-year maximum service limit in PJM closer to the limits of service for other 
ISOs (e.g., 9 years in CAISO and MISO). 
3) 
Should the Board member qualification rules be revised to provide a 
preference for some Board members that reside in the PJM region? 
X 
 
 
Comments: NGV supports PJM expressing a preference for Board members that reside 
in the PJM region; however, NGV does not support making PJM residence a 
requirement.  The Board’s purpose is not geographic representation; it is independent, 
expert governance of one of the world’s largest and most complicated organized 
electricity markets.  While residence in PJM has its benefits, the search for Board 
members should prioritize qualities such as deep electricity sector expertise and 
experience solving the challenges PJM will face over the next several years.   
4) 
Should the conflict-of-interest rules be revised to reduce the cooling off 
period for Board members from two years to one year? 
X 
 
 
Comments: NGV believes a cooling off period of one year for Board members is 
sufficient.  One year still creates meaningful separation, while two years unnecessarily 
excludes some of the candidates with the most relevant expertise.  Actual conflicts 
matter more than elapsed time.  
5) 
Should restrictions on Board communications be relaxed to enable more 
communication between the Board and stakeholders? 
 
 
 
Comments: No comments at this time. 
6) 
In order to increase transparency, should Board votes be made public or the 
Board be required to explain its reasoning?  
X 
 
 
Comments: The Board should be required to explain the rationale behind significant 
Board decisions.  This will increase transparency, increase confidence in Board 
independence, and provide important feedback to stakeholders.  NGV has no comments 
at this time regarding whether individual Board member votes should be made public.   
7) 
In order to increase transparency, should some Board meetings be open or 
available to the public? 
X

3 
 
 
Questions/Comments 
Yes No 
 
Comments: The Board’s deliberations on matters affecting PJM’s markets, transmission 
system, reliability, and consumers should generally be observable when confidentiality 
is not necessary, with non-public executive sessions reserved for times when 
confidentiality serves a legitimate governance purpose. 
8) 
Should PJM’s governing documents be revised to explicitly state that the 
responsibility of PJM and its Board is to serve the public interest? 
 
 
 
Comments: No comments at this time.  
9) 
Should state representatives have at least one voting member on the 
Nominating Committee? 
X 
 
 
Comments: Yes, states represent an interest that is not adequately captured on the 
Nominating Committee.  The Nominating Committee should include one voting 
member representing the collective PJM states.  This could help strengthen the 
legitimacy of PJM’s independent governance model and build trust between the states 
and PJM.  
10) 
Should PJM adopt public performance metrics and tie management 
compensation to their achievement? 
 
 
 
Comments: NGV needs more information on the potential metrics, how those metrics 
would be developed, and who they would apply to before forming an opinion on this 
issue.    
 
Section 205 Filing Rights 
 
 
Questions/Comments 
Yes No 
11) 
Should the stakeholder process be advisory, i.e., stakeholder votes only 
inform the Board? 
X 
 
 
Comments: PJM’s stakeholder process should provide meaningful input, technical 
expertise, and a clear measure of stakeholder support, but stakeholder votes should 
remain advisory.  
12) 
Should PJM have section 205 filing rights over the energy market and 
ancillary services unencumbered by the requirement to obtain approval of 
two-thirds of the Members Committee? 
X 
 
 
Comments: NGV supports expanding PJM’s FPA section 205 filing rights.  Giving PJM 
increased authority would expedite actions and support PJM’s ability to react to the 
dynamic changes in the market.

4 
 
 
Questions/Comments 
Yes No 
13) 
Should PJM have section 205 filing rights over Regional Transmission 
Expansion Planning (RTEP) unencumbered by the requirement to obtain 
approval of two-thirds of the Members Committee? 
X 
 
 
Comments: NGV supports expanding PJM’s FPA section 205 filing rights.  Giving PJM 
increased authority would expedite actions and support PJM’s ability to react to the 
dynamic changes in the market. 
14) 
Should the Organization of PJM States Inc (OPSI) have “jump ball” rights 
over resource adequacy and transmission cost allocation filings when a 
supermajority of OPSI agrees on an alternative proposal? 
 
X 
 
Comments: At this time, NGV does not support OPSI having jump ball rights.    
Instead, NGV supports providing adequate funding and empowerment of states to 
organize themselves through a new organization that can more meaningfully advocate 
for their interests at PJM.   
15) 
Should the Members Committee have “jump ball” filing rights over the 
portions of the tariff where PJM has 205 filing rights when a supermajority 
of stakeholders approves an alternative proposal? 
X 
 
 
Comments: A supermajority jump ball right for the Members Committee would 
appropriately balance independent PJM governance with meaningful stakeholder 
participation.  PJM’s Board should have primary responsibility for exercising PJM’s 
FPA section 205 filing rights, and ordinary stakeholder votes should remain advisory.  
However, where an alternative proposal achieves an exceptionally high level of cross-
sector stakeholder support, that consensus should have a meaningful procedural 
consequence.  Allowing both the Board proposal and the supermajority-supported 
alternative proposal to be presented to FERC preserves Board independence while 
ensuring that extraordinary stakeholder consensus cannot simply be disregarded.  FERC 
would remain the ultimate arbiter of the competing approaches. 
 
Stakeholder Process 
 
 
Questions/Comments 
Yes No 
16) 
Should the approval threshold in the Members Committee be lowered from 
two-thirds sector-weighted voting? 
 
 
 
Comments: No comments at this time. 
17) 
Should the voting rules barring affiliate votes, which apply to senior 
standing committees, also apply to lower-level committees?

5 
 
 
Questions/Comments 
Yes No 
 
Comments: No comments at this time. 
 
State Participation 
 
Questions/Comments 
Yes No 
18) 
In addition to OPSI, should there be a second state representative group 
consisting of governors’ representatives and/or state legislators’ 
representatives? 
X 
 
 
Comments: Yes.  This group could complement, not replace, OPSI by providing a state 
policy perspective that is distinct from OPSI’s remit.  The Northeast provides a useful 
model.  In ISO-NE, the New England States Committee on Electricity (“NESCOE”) 
provides a regional vehicle through which the New England governors advance their 
collective interests on regional electricity matters.  NESCOE is distinct from the New 
England Conference of Public Utility Commissioners (“NECPUC”), allowing 
governors’ energy policy perspectives and utility regulators’ perspectives to be 
represented separately.  A second state organization in PJM could also improve regional 
coordination.  PJM spans 13 states and the District of Columbia, whose policies and 
resource preferences differ substantially.  Many of PJM’s most difficult challenges 
cannot be solved effectively one state at a time.  A governors’ representative 
organization could provide a forum for states to identify areas of common interest, 
develop regional positions, and engage PJM collectively.  
19) 
Should state representatives have a formal voting role in the stakeholder 
process (limited to certain topics, such as resource adequacy and regional 
transmission cost allocation) in addition to the consumer advocate votes?   
 
 
 
Comments: No comments at this time. 
20) 
Should PJM be required to consult with OPSI prior to making a section 205 
filing related to resource adequacy and transmission cost allocation? 
 
X 
 
Comments: PJM should not be required to consult with OPSI as a procedural 
prerequisite to exercising its FPA section 205 filing rights, including with respect to 
resource adequacy or transmission cost allocation.  However, PJM should substantially 
strengthen its engagement with OPSI and other state representatives.  Improving 
transparency and demonstrating that state concerns have been meaningfully considered 
would help rebuild trust between PJM and the states without compromising PJM’s 
independence.

6 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Respectfully submitted, 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
/s/ Amber Thornhill
